etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 御(お) (o-, honorific prefix) + 負(ま)け (make, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 負(ま)ける (makeru, “to lower in price”)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Found in Hida dialect during the Edo period.
Generally considered to be a variation from どいかい (doikai), from the emphasizing prefix ど (do-, “very”) and the adjective 厳い (ikai, “great, huge, many”). The Nihon Kokugo Daijiten states that the sound change of /doikai/ → /dekai/ does not match the facts of the term's development. However, the /oi/ → /e/ sound shift is quite common in Japanese, and the question may hinge on which form appeared first, でかい (dekai) or でっかい (dekkai). If でかい (dekai) evolved from でっかい (dekkai) instead of the other way around, the do + ikai derivation would not explain the geminate /-kk-/ in でっかい (dekkai). The Nihon Kokugo Daijiten suggests an alternative derivation of でこ (deko, “hugely, enormously”, adverb; old slang or dialect term, persisting in modern でこでこ (dekodeko)) + 厳い (ikai, “great, huge, many”): */deko ikai/ → */dekoikai/ → */dekekai/ → /dekkai/ → /dekai/.
Also said to be the adjective form of でかし, from いでかす, transitive of 出で来 (ideku, “to appear”). However, the semantic development required for this is improbable, and this is more likely a folk etymology.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese 丸む (marumu), in the 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) pattern.
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: By surface analysis, 共(きょう) (kyō, “co-”) + 存(ぞん) (zon, “exist”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 叫(さけ)ぶ (sakebu, “to scream, to shout, to cry”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Derived as the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of now-obsolete verb 唾吐く (tsubaku, “to spit, to expectorate”), itself from 唾 (tsu, “saliva”) + 吐く (haku, “to expel from the mouth: to spit, to vomit, to exhale”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Appears to be a shortening of tsubaki above. Alternatively, may be a fusion of tsu below with particle は (wa, originally pa in Old Japanese, combining in some cases as ba).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Appears to be the oldest form. Possibly onomatopoeia.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: May be a Japanese coinage from Middle Chinese-derived components, as 始 (shi, “beginning”) + 末 (matsu, “end”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 山脈 (MC srean meak).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Probably from Chinese 平方 (píngfāng, literally "flat square", "flat" because it accounts for 2 dimensions only). Compare 立方 (rippō, “cube”, literally "standing square", accounting for the third dimension).
First attested in Japanese in a text from 1875.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 徴 (chō, "collect taxes or payment") + 収 (shū, "collect").

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 欲 is a daiyōji replacing 慾.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Shift from 浅(あさ)向(む)く (asamuku).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 比(ひ) (hi, “ratio”) + 率(りつ) (ritsu, “rate”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Compound of 炭 (tan, “coal”) + 素 (so, “element”), calque of Dutch koolstof (literally “coal stuff”), from German Kohlenstoff. Compare also Luxembourgish Kuelestoff, Danish kulstof.
Coined by Japanese scientist Udagawa Yōan in 1834 in his book 遠西医方名物考補遺 (“炭素”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 祈(いの)る (inoru, “to pray”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 考古(こうこ) (kōko, “archaeology”) + 学(がく) (-gaku, “study”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 自(じ) (ji, “self”) + 転(てん) (ten, “rotate; round”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, ultimately from Proto-Japonic *kusa. Found in the Man'yōshū, completed some time after 759 CE. Possibly cognate with Korean 꽃 (kkot, “flower”).
The development of the fake, amateur senses is unclear, but probably from an earlier meaning green, referring to the color of the grass.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/sau/ → /sɔː/ → /soː/
From Middle Chinese 草 (MC tshawX).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From the resemblance of multiple repetitions of w (w, “LOL”) to grass: wwwwwwwww.
Possibly influenced by the term くすくす (kusukusu), an adverb indicating stifled laughter.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese compound 要請 /要请 (ʔjiew tshjeng^X, literally “demand + request”). Compare modern Mandarin 要請／要请 (yāojí, “request; require”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 貝(かい) (kai, “shellfish”) + 殻(から) (kara, “shell”). The kara changes to gara as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 連 (ren, “consecutive”) + 休 (kyū, “day off”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 酸 (swan).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
*/pina/ → /fina/ → /hina/
Appears to be from Old Japanese. The derivative form hiwina (later hīna) appears in The Tale of Genji, dated to before 1021.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
*/pipina/ → */fifina/ → /fiwina/ → /hiːna/
Possibly an alteration of a reduplicated form hinahina.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
*/pijoko/ → /fijoko/ → /hijoko/
Compound of ひよ (piyo → hiyo, “onomatopoeia for the sound a chick makes”) + 子 (ko, “diminutive suffix”). Compare ぴよぴよ (piyopiyo, “tweet-tweet; cheep-cheep”) or peep.
Possibly related to Middle Korean 비〮육 (píywùk), whence modern Korean 병아리 (byeong'ari, “chick”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/hijoko/ → /hijokko/
Alteration of hiyoko above. The geminate kk sound emphasizes the diminutiveness.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese. Most reconstructions of the original Middle Chinese reading start with an affricate, so this Japanese reading may have come from a dialect; compare Hakka reading ts'u¹.
